books.name: Commas that Change Meaning
books.focus: Let's eat, Grandma! · eats shoots and leaves · However hard

items.s: Let's eat___ Grandma!
items.tip: A comma before the name of the person you're talking to: Let's eat, Grandma!

no.no mark: Without the comma, you're inviting everyone to eat Grandma! The comma shows you're talking TO her.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, and Grandma isn't one.
no.:: A colon would introduce what we're eating, which would be Grandma again!

items.say: Let's eat, Grandma!
items.ask: Let's eat Grandma!

items.s: Only some of us were done, so the students___ who had finished early were allowed to leave.
items.tip: No commas: who had finished early picks out WHICH students could leave.

no.,: With commas, it would mean ALL the students had finished early, but only some had.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, and the students isn't one.
no.:: A colon would introduce an explanation, but here we're saying which students.

items.say: Only some of us were done, so the students who had finished early were allowed to leave.
items.ask: Only some of us were done, so the students who had finished early were allowed to leave.

items.s: Everyone was done, so the students___ who had worked hard all morning, were allowed to leave.
items.tip: With commas, who had worked hard all morning is extra information about ALL the students.

no.no mark: There's already a closing comma, and since everyone was done, this is extra information. Open it with a comma.
no.;: A semicolon would cut off the students, which isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon would introduce an explanation, but here we're adding a fact about all of them.

items.say: Everyone was done, so the students, who had worked hard all morning, were allowed to leave.
items.ask: Everyone was done, so the students who had worked hard all morning, were allowed to leave.

items.s: My only brother___ Arjun, loves chess.
items.tip: You have only one brother, so his name is extra information: put it between commas.

no.no mark: You have only one brother, so his name doesn't pick him out. It's extra, so it goes between commas.
no.;: A semicolon would cut off My only brother, which isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. Here we just add his name.

items.say: My only brother, Arjun, loves chess.
items.ask: My only brother Arjun, loves chess.

items.s: I have three friends here today; my friend___ Arjun is the one in the red cap.
items.tip: No commas: Arjun picks out WHICH of your friends you mean.

no.,: With commas, Arjun would sound like your only friend. Here the name picks out which friend, so no commas.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, and my friend isn't one.
no.:: A colon would introduce an explanation, but here the name says which friend.

items.say: I have three friends here today; my friend Arjun is the one in the red cap.
items.ask: I have three friends here today; my friend Arjun is the one in the red cap.

items.s: The panda eats___ shoots and leaves.
items.tip: No comma: the panda simply eats shoots and leaves (bamboo!).

no.,: With a comma, the panda eats, then shoots and leaves the café, like a cowboy! Without it, it simply eats shoots and leaves.
no.;: A semicolon would make shoots and leaves a separate sentence, but it has no subject.
no.:: A colon would introduce a list, but shoots and leaves are already what it eats.

items.say: The panda eats shoots and leaves.
items.ask: The panda eats shoots and leaves.

items.s: However___ hard we tried, the kite wouldn't fly.
items.tip: However hard = no matter how hard. There's no comma after However here.

no.,: With a comma, However would mean 'but', and hard we tried makes no sense. However hard = no matter how hard.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, and However isn't one.
no.:: A colon would introduce an explanation, but However hard belongs together.

items.say: However hard we tried, the kite wouldn't fly.
items.ask: However hard we tried, the kite wouldn't fly.

items.s: However___ we tried again the next day, and it flew!
items.tip: Here However means 'but', so it needs a comma after it.

no.no mark: Here However means 'but'. With no comma, it reads like 'However we tried' = in whatever way we tried.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, and However isn't one.
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation, but However is just a linking word here.

items.say: However, we tried again the next day, and it flew!
items.ask: However we tried again the next day, and it flew!

books.name: Hyphen Detectives
books.focus: hyphens that change meaning: man-eating, re-signed, twenty-odd, co-op

items.s: The aquarium has a ___ shark!
items.tip: man-eating = it eats people. Without the hyphen, a man eating shark is a man who is eating shark!

no.man eating: A man eating shark is a man who is eating shark meat! Join the describing words: man-eating.
no.man's-eating: There's no apostrophe in this describing word: man-eating.
no.maneating: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.

items.say: The aquarium has a man-eating shark!
items.ask: The aquarium has a man-eating shark!

items.s: We had to ___ the old sofa with new fabric.
items.tip: re-cover = cover again. recover = get better, or get something back.

no.recover: recover means get better or get something back. To cover it again, write re-cover.
no.re cover: re isn't a word on its own. Join it with a hyphen: re-cover.
no.re-covers: After had to we need the base form: re-cover.

items.say: We had to re-cover the old sofa with new fabric.
items.ask: We had to re-cover the old sofa with new fabric.

items.s: ___ students turned up to the chess club, so we needed more boards.
items.tip: twenty-odd = about twenty. twenty odd students = twenty strange students!

no.Twenty odd: Twenty odd students means twenty strange students! For 'about twenty', write Twenty-odd.
no.Twentyodd: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.

items.say: Twenty-odd students turned up to the chess club, so we needed more boards.
items.ask: Twenty-odd students turned up to the chess club, so we needed more boards.

items.s: We followed a ___ path that hardly anyone walks on.
items.tip: little-used = not used much. A little used path could mean a small, used path.

no.little used: Without the hyphen it can mean a small path that has been used. For 'hardly used', write little-used.
no.littleused: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.
no.little-use: It describes the path, so we need the -ed form: little-used.

items.say: We followed a little-used path that hardly anyone walks on.
items.ask: We followed a little-used path that hardly anyone walks on.

items.s: The goalkeeper ___ for another season, and the fans cheered.
items.tip: re-signed = signed again (a new contract). resigned = quit!

no.resigned: resigned means quit, and the fans wouldn't cheer for that! Signed again → re-signed.
no.re signed: re isn't a word on its own. Join it with a hyphen: re-signed.
no.re-sign: The sentence is in the past: re-signed.

items.say: The goalkeeper re-signed for another season, and the fans cheered.
items.ask: The goalkeeper re-signed for another season, and the fans cheered.

items.s: Our coach is a ___ chess player.
items.tip: world-class describes the player as one idea, so it takes a hyphen.

no.world class: Before a noun, world and class work as one describing word, so join them: world-class.
no.worldclass: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.
no.world's-class: There's no apostrophe in this describing word: world-class.

items.say: Our coach is a world-class chess player.
items.ask: Our coach is a world-class chess player.

items.s: The chickens sleep safely in their ___ at night.
items.tip: A coop is a chickens' house. A co-op is a shop or group owned by its members.

no.co-op: A co-op is a shop or club owned by its members. A chickens' house is a coop.
no.co op: co isn't a word on its own. A chickens' house is a coop.
no.coops: their coop is one house for the chickens, so no -s here.

items.say: The chickens sleep safely in their coop at night.
items.ask: The chickens sleep safely in their coop at night.

items.s: The librarian asked us to ___ the books by author.
items.tip: re-sort = sort again. resort = a holiday place (or to resort to something).

no.resort: A resort is a holiday place! To sort again, write re-sort.
no.re sort: re isn't a word on its own. Join it with a hyphen: re-sort.
no.re-sorts: After asked us to we need the base form: re-sort.

items.say: The librarian asked us to re-sort the books by author.
items.ask: The librarian asked us to re-sort the books by author.

books.name: Pixie Polish
books.focus: joint and separate owners · geese's · twins' · Whose · a question to the end

items.s: Tom___ and Mia's treehouse is the one they built together.
items.tip: One thing owned together: only the last name takes 's. Tom and Mia's treehouse.

no.'s: Tom's and Mia's would mean two different treehouses. They built ONE together, so only Mia's takes 's.
no.s': Tom is one person, so s' doesn't fit, and only the last name takes 's anyway.
no.,: A comma would split Tom from Mia's treehouse.

items.say: Tom and Mia's treehouse is the one they built together.
items.ask: Tom and Mia's treehouse is the one they built together.

items.s: Tom's and Mia___ bikes are different colours.
items.tip: Two separate things (a bike each): both names take 's. Tom's and Mia's bikes.

no.no mark: With separate things (two bikes, one each), both names need 's: Tom's and Mia's.
no.s': Mia is one person, so it's Mia's, not Mias'.
no.s: Mias isn't a name. To show the bike is hers, write Mia's.

items.say: Tom's and Mia's bikes are different colours.
items.ask: Tom's and Mia's bikes are different colours.

items.s: All three ___ honking woke the whole campsite.
items.tip: geese is a plural without s, so add 's: the geese's honking.

no.geeses': geese is already plural, so we don't add s. Just 's: geese's.
no.goose's: goose's is one goose, but All three means three geese.
no.geeses: geeses isn't a word. The plural of goose is geese.

items.say: All three geese's honking woke the whole campsite.
items.ask: All three geese's honking woke the whole campsite.

items.s: Isn't it amazing that octopuses can change colour___
items.tip: It starts with Isn't it…, so however long it gets, it's a question.

The sentence starts with Isn't it…, so it's a question, even though it's long.
no.,: A comma can't end a sentence.
no.;: A semicolon needs another full sentence after it.

items.say: Isn't it amazing that octopuses can change colour?
items.ask: Isn't it amazing that octopuses can change colour

items.s: The shop sells two- and ___ bikes.
items.tip: two- and three-wheeled: the first hyphen 'hangs', waiting for the same ending.

no.three wheeled: The hanging hyphen in two- needs a partner: three-wheeled.
no.three-wheel-ed: -ed is part of the word wheeled. It doesn't get its own hyphen.
no.threewheeled: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.

items.say: The shop sells two- and three-wheeled bikes.
items.ask: The shop sells two- and three-wheeled bikes.

items.s: Seeing the northern lights was a ___ experience.
items.tip: A long describing phrase before a noun is joined with hyphens: a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

no.once in a lifetime: Before the noun (experience), the whole phrase works as one describing word, so it takes hyphens.
no.once-in-a lifetime: Every word in the phrase is joined: once-in-a-lifetime.
no.once-in-a-life-time: lifetime is one word, so no hyphen inside it.

items.say: Seeing the northern lights was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
items.ask: Seeing the northern lights was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

items.s: The ___ birthday party is on Saturday; both of them are turning twelve.
items.tip: both of them = two twins, a plural ending in s, so the apostrophe goes after the s: twins'.

no.twin's: twin's means one twin, but both of them are turning twelve: twins'.
no.twins: twins (no apostrophe) doesn't show that the party is theirs.
no.twins's: After a plural ending in s, add only the apostrophe: twins'.

items.say: The twins' birthday party is on Saturday; both of them are turning twelve.
items.ask: The twins' birthday party is on Saturday; both of them are turning twelve.

items.s: ___ turn is it to feed the fish?
items.tip: Whose = belonging to which person. Who's always means who is or who has.

no.Who's: Who's means who is: Who is turn is it? No! For 'belonging to which person', write Whose.
no.Whos: Whos isn't a word. Belonging to which person → Whose.

items.say: Whose turn is it to feed the fish?
items.ask: Whose turn is it to feed the fish?
